Quarterly review of the storage estate

The estate now holds forty-one terabytes across six drives, of which roughly
nine are believed to be duplicated. That figure is an estimate and should be
treated as one: it comes from sampling three directories and extrapolating,
which is a method that flatters itself.

Three things drove the growth. Every laptop retired since the second quarter
was archived whole rather than selectively, on the reasonable grounds that
deciding what to keep costs more than the disk does. Phone backups were taken
monthly and never pruned, so a photograph taken once exists in every backup
made after it. And the shared drive was migrated twice, each time by copying
rather than moving, because a copy is reversible and a move is not.

None of these decisions was wrong when it was made. Together they produced an
archive nobody can describe, which is a different kind of problem from an
archive that is merely large.

The recommendation is not to sort the estate. That would take a person a month
and produce judgements nobody could later reconstruct. The recommendation is to
find the files that are provably the same file, remove those without ceremony,
and then look at what remains. Provable duplication is a much smaller claim
than similarity, and it is one a machine can make honestly.

Anything beyond that should be presented for review rather than acted on. The
cost of deleting one unique file is not symmetrical with the benefit of
reclaiming a gigabyte, and any process that treats those two as comparable will
eventually destroy something that mattered.
